source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024)
finding: Gap 1 and 10. Asking a model to review and revise its own answer, with no outside signal, does not raise reasoning accuracy and often lowers it. Revision only helps when real external feedback (a checker, a tool, an oracle) is present.
numbers: Llama-2 (Table 6): GSM8K standard 62.0, after self-correct round 1 43.5 and round 2 36.5 (one feedback prompt); CommonSenseQA 64.0 to 37.5 and 36.5. GPT-4-Turbo (Table 5): GSM8K standard 91.5, self-correct 88.0 to 91.0 (flat or down); CommonSenseQA standard 84.0, self-correct 74.5 to 83.5.
quote: LLMs struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback, and at times, their performance even degrades
limits: Reasoning tasks with a known answer, not plans. Authors note that gains in earlier papers came from oracle labels or weak initial prompts. Tests only same-model critique.
agent_relevance: A simulate-then-revise loop where the critic is the same model reading its own plan is not evidence of improvement. Only a simulator that returns a real signal (code, rules engine, ground-truth score) justifies a revision step.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024) (multi-agent debate vs self-consistency)
finding: Gap 1, 4. Replication of Du et al. multi-agent debate on the full GSM8K test set with gpt-3.5-turbo-0301 (3 agents, 2 rounds). The debate gain is no larger than simple majority voting over the same number of samples. The authors say the gain is consistency, not critique.
numbers: Table 7 GSM8K: standard 76.7 (1 response); self-consistency 82.5 (3 responses), 85.3 (6), 88.2 (9); debate round 1 slightly above self-consistency at 3 responses, debate round 2 83.2 at 6 responses vs self-consistency 85.3 at 6 (the column layout is garbled in text, so read as approximate).
limits: One model family, one benchmark, math. Debate may differ on open plans with no single right answer.
agent_relevance: Same-model role dialog should be compared against majority of k independent samples at equal calls. Expect the vote to win or tie.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Gap 2 and 1. With an automatic verifier, coverage (any sample correct) climbs almost log-linearly over four orders of magnitude of samples. Without a verifier, majority vote and reward models plateau after about 100 samples.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% at 1 sample to 56% at 250 (prior single-sample best 43%). CodeContests Gemma-2B: 0.02% at 1 sample to 7.1% at 10,000. MATH Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000, but majority vote or reward model only 40.50% to 41.41% over the same range.
quote: common methods for picking from a sample collection (majority voting and reward models) plateau
limits: Verifiable domains (code, proofs) dominate the gains. Plans in a wargame lack a cheap exact verifier, which is the hard case the paper flags.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: for a simulated evaluator, more samples help only if the verdict check is exact. For soft plan verdicts, expect a plateau by about 100 samples; test k of 3 to 10 first. The simulation must produce a checkable outcome.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Gap 1 and 2. How best to spend test-time compute depends on prompt difficulty. Adaptive allocation between verifier search and sequential revision beats a fixed best-of-N. On problems where a small model has a non-trivial success rate, test-time compute can beat a 14 times larger model at matched FLOPs.
numbers: Compute-optimal strategy improves efficiency by more than 4x over a best-of-N baseline; FLOPs-matched win against a 14x larger model (PaLM 2-S*, MATH, trained process reward model).
limits: Needs a trained verifier. On the hardest problems extra test-time compute did not substitute for a stronger base model.
agent_relevance: Allocate simulation passes by difficulty: few for easy plan checks, more for hard ones. A router decides when to simulate.

source: Gou et al. (2024) CRITIC: Large Language Models Can Self-Correct with Tool-Interactive Critiquing
finding: Gap 1 and 10. Critique with tools (search API, code interpreter, toxicity scorer) then revise works across tasks. The paper also reports that external feedback matters: the variant with no tool (CRITIC w/o Tool) is included as an ablation, and the authors state that unreliable self-feedback may give modest gains or hurt.
numbers: ChatGPT: CRITIC gives 7.7 F1 gain over baselines across three QA tasks (500 sampled validation items each: AmbigNQ, TriviaQA, HotpotQA); self-consistency baseline used 10 samples (OpenAI) or 20 (LLaMA-2).
quote: external feedback may yield modest improvements or even deteriorate performance
limits: QA, program and toxicity tasks, not plans. The tool is a retrieval or execution check, which a plan simulator would have to imitate. Ablation numbers were not read.
agent_relevance: Revision with an external executable check is supported; revision from internal critique is not. Our simulate step should call code or a rules table when possible.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
finding: Gap 3. A strong LLM judge agrees with human preference at over 80%, the same rate as two humans agree with each other. But it shows position bias, verbosity bias, self-enhancement bias and weak reasoning when grading math.
numbers: Over 80% agreement of GPT-4 with controlled and crowdsourced human votes on MT-bench and Chatbot Arena; most judges favour the first position.
quote: LLM-as-a-judge is a scalable and explainable way to approximate human preferences
limits: Pairwise chat answers, not multi-turn plan outcomes or rule-based adjudication. Says nothing about wargame adjudication, so gap 3 stays open for plans.
agent_relevance: If a model adjudicates simulated outcomes, swap order, use another model family, and give it a code check for numbers. Agreement with humans on chat does not transfer to plan drift.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) When A Helpful Assistant Is Not Really Helpful: Personas in System Prompts Do Not Improve Performances of LLMs
finding: Gap 7. Across 162 personas, 4 model families and 2,410 factual questions, adding a persona does not improve accuracy over no persona. Effects exist but are small and inconsistent. Picking the best persona per question works about as well as random choice.
numbers: 162 roles (6 relationship types, 8 expertise domains); 2,410 questions; mixed-effects regression with model as random effect; gender-neutral roles slightly better than gendered, masculine slightly above feminine, small effect sizes; best-role-per-question search offers limited if any gain over a random role.
limits: Factual multiple-choice accuracy, not goals or behaviour in simulation. Says personas do not add knowledge. Does not say they cannot change stance or style.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on an expert persona to improve plan quality. Use personas only to set goals and constraints for a simulated actor, and test that separately.

source: Hu and Collier (2024) Quantifying the Persona Effect in LLM Simulations (ACL 2024)
finding: Gap 7. Persona variables (who the annotator is) explain under 10% of variance in human annotations on subjective NLP datasets. Prompting with them gives modest but significant gains, largest where annotators disagree mildly. A 70B model in zero-shot captured 81% of the variance achievable by a linear regression on true labels.
numbers: Persona variance explained below 10%; 81% ceiling capture for the 70B model; the stronger the correlation between persona and label, the more accurate the LLM.
quote: persona variables account for <10% variance in annotations
limits: Annotation tasks, not strategy play. Gains come only when the persona variable predicts the human response.
agent_relevance: Partly resolves Lamparth vs Snow Globe: a persona changes output only where it carries real information about the target behaviour. A goal-stating persona does, a vague background mostly does not. Not a direct test in wargames.

source: Mukobi et al. (2023) Welfare Diplomacy: Benchmarking Language Model Cooperation
finding: Gap 4. Exploiters built from a trained RL policy (a Standard Diplomacy policy, FPPI-2) joined as one or two players, played as a GPT-4 agent first, then switched to the RL policy late to take supply centres. LLM agents were highly exploitable and did not punish defectors. The adversary was code and RL, not a second LLM prompt.
numbers: Exploiter switches when other players hold ten or fewer units or after three years; exploitability measured with one and two exploiters; one exploitation experiment per set, so intervals understate uncertainty; GPT-4 root Nash welfare fell when it played the exploiter role.
quote: they still lack the cooperative capability to punish defectors
limits: No same-model adversary arm in the same experiment, so it does not show different-model beats same-model. It shows a code-built adversary finds flaws that LLM self-play did not.
agent_relevance: Supports building the red-team step from code or rules where possible. Gap 4 only partly closed.

source: Hegazy (2024) Diversity of Thought Elicits Stronger Reasoning Capabilities in Multi-Agent Debate Frameworks
finding: Gap 4. Debate among three different model families beat debate among three copies of one model on math. After four rounds a mix of Gemini-Pro, Mixtral 8x7B and PaLM 2-M reached 91% on GSM-8K.
numbers: Single models 78%, 64%, 70%. Diverse trio 78% to 91% after 4 rounds. Three Gemini-Pro copies 78% to 80% (no chain of thought) and 82% (zero-shot chain of thought). ASDiv diverse trio 94% (singles 89, 86, 81).
limits: Single-author journal paper, single run per cell, math with known answers. No equal-sample majority vote baseline, so by Huang the gain may partly be voting over a stronger mix.
agent_relevance: Evidence for a different-model critic, with the caveat that the comparator was not equal-call self-consistency. Use a second model family for the opponent or checker where cost allows.

source: Cranfield repository entry: Yuksek, Guner, Karali, Candan, Inalhan (2023) Intelligent wargaming approach to increase course of action effectiveness in military operations (AIAA 2023-2531)
finding: Gap 6. The study proposes an intelligent wargaming approach for course-of-action analysis in the military decision-making process. Plan effectiveness is scored by operational success and survivability of assets, with a fleet composer algorithm tuned by hyperparameter search. Full text could not be read: the repository returned 403 and a Cloudflare challenge, which was not bypassed.
numbers: None read. Search summary only: three stated contributions (faster COA analysis giving more candidate COAs, tactics against opposing forces, a visual wargame frame for small operator teams).
limits: Search summary only. No numbers, no sample size. Not shown as a test against human judgement or ground truth.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open. Treat as a design reference for scoring plans by mission success and asset survival, not as evidence.

source: Status of gaps 5, 8 and 9 (no new sources opened)
finding: Gaps 5, 8, 9. The arXiv API returned HTTP 429, the OpenAlex daily budget was exhausted, Semantic Scholar returned 429, and the shared WebSearch budget ran out after one query. No 2026 replication of the Rivera or Lamparth protocols, no counterfactual-sensitivity study, and no new RAND or RSAS source could be found or opened.
limits: Absence is due to tool limits, not proof that nothing exists.
agent_relevance: These gaps stay open and should be rerun when search budget is available.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) MT-Bench paper, self-enhancement bias section
finding: Gap 3 and 4. The authors name self-enhancement bias (a judge favouring answers from its own family) but say a controlled study is hard to run. Suggests a same-model adjudicator or adversary may under-penalise flaws that look like its own output, but this is not measured cleanly.
numbers: No clean effect size; position bias is strong in most judges.
limits: Mixed evidence, not a measured effect size.
agent_relevance: Use a different family for the judge step when cost allows, and swap answer order.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys, cost note
finding: Gap 2. Repeated sampling can lower cost. At a fixed FLOP budget, many samples from a smaller model can cover more problems than fewer samples from a larger one on some sets (for example MATH).
numbers: Coverage is maximised by a smaller model on some datasets at constant FLOPs; the paper also tests an agent framework with Claude 3.5 Sonnet on SWE-bench Lite.
limits: Needs a verifier; cost parity depends on price per token as well as FLOPs.
agent_relevance: Median of k cheap simulated runs may beat one expensive run only if the verdict is exact. Otherwise test at equal tokens.

source: Huang et al. (2024), advice on fair comparison
finding: Gap 10. The paper says to compare self-correction against self-consistency at equal numbers of responses and to put equal effort into the prompts of both arms. Gains reported elsewhere often vanish under this rule.
numbers: No new numbers; see d01 and d02.
agent_relevance: A reflection slot must be tested against a same-budget baseline and scored on ground truth, not on whether the model followed the instruction to reflect. Gap 10 stays open for wargames.
